content:
While writing some metaprograms, I've come across a few completely trivial "issues" in various random parts of the codebase. Even calling them issues feels like hyperbole, as they're mostly things like single-letter typos in docstrings, and at worst they make discerning what the particular piece of code is doing slightly more difficult.
I'd like to point these out / fix them, but I don't know what the protocol for such trivial changes is, since none of them in any way justify opening a pull request, given how swamped the project already is in pull requests.
Is there some kind of existing protocol for getting these fixed?
I didn't know where else to ask so i figured this is as good a place as any.
leanprover/lean4 ? If so, I believe PRs fixing typos are welcome without an RFC, but I am not part of the Lean FRO, so take my advice with a pinch of salt

I have exactly two PRs to leanprover/lean4 and they're both fixing textual errors in docstrings. If it objectively improves readability (without adding clutter) I don't see why it "doesn't justify opening a PR"!
Because https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md tells you not to do that.
The contributing guidelines tell you to submit an RFC, but on the other hand, I've been told by Joachim before that it can be ok to apply common sense for PRs that are not crazy ideas.
I strongly expect that the privilege of making exceptions to this rule is not transitive.

Without knowing the protocol myself, that CONTRIBUTING.md reads to me like "You must open an issue before a PR, if the PR is adding a feature then your issue must be an RFC and follow some guidelines on RFCs" ... leaving implied, by omission, that for 'trivial' fixes (without a new feature), the issue format is much more flexible and doesn't need to be an RFC.

Is that accurate?
